sections.h2: Which offices handle property tax in Hopkins County, KY?
sections.html:
The Property Valuation Administrator values every parcel in Hopkins County, and the Sheriff's Office collects the bills. The PVA is in the Courthouse Annex at 25 East Center Street, Madisonville, KY 42431, phone (270) 821-3092. It lists property, assesses it and prepares the tax roll, which the public can inspect.

The Sheriff's Office is at 261 Responders Lane in Madisonville, phone 270-821-5661, open Monday through Friday from 8 AM to 4 PM. After April 15 the unpaid bills belong to the Hopkins County Clerk at 270-326-2097.

Tax bills are issued in the name of the owner on January 1 of the tax year. If you bought in the spring, the previous owner may receive the bill and should forward it. The Sheriff does not see new deed transfers, so a buyer who gets no bill can call the office or print one from its website.

sections.h2: When are Hopkins County property tax bills due?
sections.html:
Bills usually go out around September 30, and collection opens October 1. The Sheriff's own calendar sets the stages.

Hopkins County Sheriff collection calendar (source: Hopkins County Sheriff's Office)
PeriodAmount due
October 1 to November 12 percent discount
November 2 to December 31Face amount
January 1 to January 315 percent penalty added
February 1 to April 1521 percent added

The Sheriff lists 21 percent for that last stretch. KRS 134.015 sets a 10 percent penalty after January, and the Department of Revenue's explainer shows a Sheriff's add-on fee and commission as well, so ask the Sheriff's Office for an exact payoff before paying in February or March.

Collection ends at close of business on April 15 under state law. Whatever is still open then goes to the County Clerk's office.

sections.h2: How do I pay a Hopkins County tax bill?
sections.html:
You can pay online or at the Sheriff's office, and the Sheriff takes full payments only. A partial payment is not accepted.

  • Accepted forms: cash, check, money order, cashier's check and credit card.
  • Cards are run by a third party, and the convenience fee is 2.5 percent plus 30 cents.
  • Online checks carry a $1.50 processing fee.
  • Make checks payable to Hopkins County Sheriff.

If a mortgage servicer escrows your taxes, the Sheriff points out that getting the bill to the lender is the owner's job. A servicer cannot pay a bill it never received.

sections.h2: How is a Hopkins County tax bill figured and split at closing?
sections.html:
Divide the taxable assessment by 100 and multiply by the current tax rate. The result is the amount owed, less any volunteer fire department fee or watershed tax that may apply to your parcel.

For a sale, the Sheriff offers a simple proration. Take the prior year's bill, divide by 365 to get a daily cost, and multiply by the days the seller occupied the house. A seller who held the home through June 30, for example, would owe about 181 days of the daily amount.

Closing agents sometimes use the actual bill once it is out. Compare their figure with the Sheriff's method before signing the settlement statement.

sections.h2: How can I appeal a Hopkins County assessment?
sections.html:
You must talk to the PVA first. KRS 133.120 requires a conference with the PVA or a deputy before or during the inspection period, and a phone conference is allowed on request.

  • At the conference, the PVA explains how the value was reached and keeps a written record.
  • If you remain unhappy, file a letter or petition with the County Clerk by one workday after the inspection period ends.
  • Give your opinion of fair cash value and bring facts: land and building details, insurance, construction costs, listings or sales and loans.
  • Appear at the hearing in person or through an authorized representative.

The board denies an appeal if you do not supply reasonable information it requests. Taxes stay due on the value you claim while the appeal runs.

sections.h2: What exemptions apply to a Hopkins County home or farm?
sections.html:
Hopkins County follows the state homestead exemption of $49,100 for 2025 and 2026. It applies to owners aged 65 or older, or those totally disabled, who live in the home as their primary residence.

Against the Census median home value of $142,800, the exemption would leave a taxable base of $93,700. The application is filed in person at the PVA office with proof of age, and most people use a birth certificate or driver's license. Disability claims require records showing payments from January through December.

Farm owners have another route. State law values agricultural land by its production capability rather than market value, and the Sheriff's page describes qualifying parcels as ten or more acres used for livestock or crops, including timber. A person may claim only one exemption on one property in one county and state.

sections.h2: What if I sell a Hopkins County house with unpaid property tax?
sections.html:
Unpaid tax follows the parcel. After April 15 the bill becomes a certificate of delinquency filed at the Hopkins County Clerk's office, and a lien is recorded against the property.

The Clerk's 2025 tax sale shows how the next stage works. The sale ran October 8, 2025, electronically from 24 Union Street in Madisonville, and buyers paid a registration fee of $5 per priority bill or $10 per current-year bill, capped at $250 combined. The Clerk's own paperwork warned that buyers who missed payment deadlines forfeited their bills.

A purchased certificate can carry the buyer's fees on top of the county's. Clearing the account with the Sheriff before the deadline, or the Clerk afterward, saves those costs. Ask the Clerk's office for current delinquent amounts, since the Sheriff's website and the Clerk's website do not link to each other.

sections.h2: What is Hopkins County, Kentucky, like for a home seller?
sections.html:
Hopkins County lies in western Kentucky, with Madisonville as county seat and its largest city. It was created on December 9, 1806 from Henderson County, and it covers 542 square miles of land. The Pond River, Tradewater River and Green River cross it, and the terrain turns hilly in the south and center.

Coal mining in the south and farming in the north shaped the economy. Soybeans, corn and tobacco are the main crops, and the Pennyrile Parkway and Western Kentucky Parkway both run through the county. Other cities include Dawson Springs, Earlington, Nortonville, Mortons Gap, Hanson, White Plains, Nebo and St. Charles.

  • 2025 population estimate: 45,127, down 0.6 percent from 2020.
  • Median owner-occupied home value: $142,800.
  • Owner-occupied rate: 70.7 percent.
  • Median household income: $56,815.
  • Median gross rent: $837.

Hopkins County Schools serves most of the county, and Dawson Springs has its own independent district.

faqs.q: When does the Hopkins County Sheriff start collecting property tax?
faqs.a: Collection normally begins October 1, with bills mailed around September 30. A 2 percent discount applies through November 1, and the face amount is due through December 31.

faqs.q: Can I make partial payments on a Hopkins County tax bill?
faqs.a: No. The Sheriff requires payment in full. Online, cash, check, money order, cashier's check and credit card payments are all accepted, with a processor fee on cards.

faqs.q: Who gets the bill if I just bought a house in Hopkins County?
faqs.a: The bill goes to whoever owned the parcel on January 1. If the seller receives it, they should pass it on. A buyer without a bill can call the Sheriff at 270-821-5661 or print a copy from the website.

faqs.q: Where do I go after April 15 if I still owe?
faqs.a: Contact the Hopkins County Clerk, since the Sheriff transfers all unpaid bills there at the close of business on April 15. The Clerk's number on the Sheriff's page is 270-326-2097.

faqs.q: Is there a tax break for older Hopkins County homeowners?
faqs.a: Yes. Owners 65 or older who live in the home can claim the state homestead exemption of $49,100, filed through the PVA at 25 East Center Street. Totally disabled owners qualify as well.
